translations: It left the open sea and came to a high cliff at the edge of the North Sea. The wind would rise as it passed over the mountain wall, and then fall on the other side. The giant bird, Peng, didn't rush to charge into the clouds; instead, it stretched out one wing to feel the wind. When the wind dissipated, it retracted its wing and settled down.
A few small birds flew over and saw the giant bird standing still, so they asked it why it wasn't flying.
The small birds laughed and said, "We can fly whenever we want; why do we need to wait?"

Peng looked at them as they nimbly turned around the cliff, but it didn't argue. The small birds' wings were suited for the valley in front of them, and a gentle breeze was enough to lift them. However, Peng wasn't heading for the nearby treetops or taking a short route that would bring it back after circling the cliff.

The small birds demonstrated how to use the wind between the treetops to turn. Peng watched carefully and learned to retract its wings to let the wind carry it, rather than just using its vast size to overpower everything. Its new form brought it strength, but not all the experience it needed; acknowledging what it didn't know made each attempt yield new results.
One small bird kindly taught it to flap its wings faster. Peng tried it lightly, and suddenly a strong gust of wind blew, sending the small birds tumbling onto the leeward rocks.
The lead bird smoothed its feathers and changed its tune: "You'd better learn slowly. Our methods don't seem to be big enough for you."

Peng folded its wings and slowly settled on the sea surface, like a silent mountain. It no longer rushed forward whenever it saw a gust of wind, nor did it repeatedly charge into the sky from the same rock, just to show off its newfound ability to fly. Now, its scales had transformed into soft feathers, its back was as wide as Mount Tai, and its wingtips stretched towards the sky like clouds hanging from the heavens. Its gaze was no longer restless, but instead, it calmly looked out at the vast North Sea, as if pondering how to interact with the world in its new form.

At that moment, Aman stood on a rock at the edge of the North Sea, holding a rough bamboo staff and muttering to himself: "This guy knows how to 'fold its wings,' but it's not as good as folding up its stall." He looked up at Peng and tried to point out the wind direction with his staff, but accidentally poked a sleeping sea star, which flipped over and made a soft "hissing" sound. Aman scowled and grumbled, "Don't say I didn't warn you; even the sea star is afraid of me." This remark made the nearby fish stifle their giggles, and the water's surface rippled with fine waves, as if they were teasing the self-proclaimed recorder.

Peng's chest fins trembled gently, and the seawater behind it churned up layers of waves, as if the wind between heaven and earth was brewing. It closed its eyes, feeling the ancient wind rising from the depths of the North Sea – the wind that carried the breath of the tides and the call of the South Sea. The wind burst forth from the sea surface, passing through its feathers like an invisible palm caressing its back. Peng's feathers quivered in the wind, like clouds being gently stirred.

Aman saw this and couldn't help but shout, "Oh no, this wind is really strong; it's going to blow my beard away!" He grabbed his chin with his hand and struck a comical pose, as if being blown away by the wind. The fish in the water burst into laughter, releasing bubbles and making "gurgling" sounds. Although Aman's antics were somewhat ridiculous, they didn't affect Peng's decision. With the wind's support, it slowly rose, its back carrying the sky, its wings spread like clouds, and it gradually left the sea surface behind.

As Peng's figure completely left the water's surface, transforming into a huge white silhouette heading towards the South Sea, the creatures of the North Sea were still whispering among themselves. Some said, "It grew wings but still stayed here; the change seems useless." Others shook their heads, "Wait until it truly flies away, and then we'll know the value of those wings." Aman, meanwhile, stood on the rock, his bamboo staff blowing in the wind, and he quietly recorded: "Peng is no longer a kun, its wings are like clouds hanging from the sky, riding the June wind, carrying the sky, and flying towards the South Sea Heaven Pool." His pen scratched out a few lines on the damp stone, conveying surprise and awe, but without any explanation or guidance.

And so, the North Sea's surface returned to calm, with only the distant wind whispering a gentle farewell to the giant bird that had just completed its transformation into Peng. Its figure disappeared into the distance, eventually becoming a faint cloud shadow that vanished into the vast sky leading to the South Sea Heaven Pool.

Initially, the creatures of the North Sea thought that since Peng had grown wings, it should have disappeared into the horizon. When it remained, some said the transformation was useless. Peng didn't let these judgments rush it. Between being able to fly and being suited for long-distance travel, there was still a gap in understanding the wind and direction.

At sunset, the wind on the sea surface weakened. Peng stood at a high point, watching as the clouds continued to flow south. It knew that a greater wind would form between heaven and earth, one that could support its broad wings and carry it beyond the North Sea to truly distant places.

Before that wind arrived, stopping wasn't a retreat to its fish form, and waiting wasn't giving up on its journey. Peng folded its wings and, for the first time, quietly stood guard at the high point of the North Sea.
